lesson.title: -ieren Verb Builder
lesson.subtitle: -ate, -ize, -ify → -ieren: the factory that turns English verbs into German

hook.title: The Verb Factory
hook.content: English borrowed its intellectual verbs from Latin and French — analyze, organize, copy, produce. German borrowed the exact same loans, then stamped one native suffix on them: -ieren. Because both languages took the same Latin parts, every English -ate/-ize verb you own already exists in German with a German ending. This lesson is the assembly manual: copy → kopieren, produce → produzieren, correct → korrigieren, reduce → reduzieren, activate → aktivieren. You are not learning 500 verbs. You are learning one stamp.

footnotes.title: The z You Can Hear
footnotes.content: Watch -ize verbs: the z of English -ize becomes German s before -ieren (organize → organisieren, realize → realisieren). And -ify verbs grow a full -ifizieren: identify → identifizieren, verify → verifizieren. The Latin soft c [ts] lives inside both.

pattern.title: Three Formulas, Five Hundred Verbs
pattern.content: Formula one — -ate → -ieren: reserve → reservieren, activate → aktivieren, inform → informieren (and argue → argumentieren — the -ate vanished into the stamp). Formula two — -ize → -isieren: organize → organisieren. But watch the -ce words: produce keeps its z — produzieren, reduce → reduzieren. Formula three — -ify → -ifizieren: identify → identifizieren. The one iron rule: stress lands on the -IE- (stu-DIE-ren, ko-PIE-ren) and never moves, no matter how long the verb gets.
pattern.linguist_note: The stress rule is why -ieren verbs reject ge- (next lesson) and why you can always hear a -ieren verb in fast speech: the long German [iː] of -IE- rings out like a bell in every sentence.

exercises.explanation: The -ize becomes -is-: organis- + -ieren = organisieren. No ge- belongs on a -ieren verb.

exercises.prompt: Run the stamp over the Latin loans:
exercises.target_answer: kopieren, produzieren, korrigieren, reduzieren, fotografieren, argumentieren
exercises.meaning: to copy, to produce, to correct, to reduce, to photograph, to argue
exercises.explanation: Same Latin roots, same English words, one German suffix: -ieren — the camera verb included (Foto is German's word for photo).

exercises.prompt: Where does the stress land in 'studieren'?
options: German -ieren verbs have no fixed stress
exercises.meaning: Suffix stress is the password of -ieren verbs
exercises.explanation: The stress always lands on -IE- — and that fixed stress is exactly what blocks ge- in the participle.

exercises.prompt: Run the stamp: English 'to activate' → German:
exercises.explanation: activate → aktiv- + -ieren = aktivieren. The Latin c turned k on German pages.

vocab_hints.note: Tisch is masculine — the Him-Case adds -en: ein → einen

exercises.explanation: Verb in position 2 with wir, direct object with the masculine accusative: 'Wir reservieren einen Tisch'.

summary.outcome: Derive German -ieren verbs from English -ate/-ize/-ify verbs and stress them correctly.
summary.takeaway: English -ate/-ize/-ify and German -ieren/-isieren/-ifizieren are one Latin loan wearing two flags — stress stays on -IE-.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the No-ge- Club — why 'gestudiert' is impossible and 'studiert' is the law.

reparieren.context_translation: I have to repair the television.

funktionieren.etymology_derivation: Used specifically for machines and mechanisms functioning properly.

kapieren.context_translation: Did you get it / grasp it?
kapieren.etymology_derivation: From Latin capere (to seize/capture). Mental grasp.

akzeptieren.etymology_derivation: Latin acceptare (hard c → k, soft c → z [ts]).

reservieren.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.

reduzieren.context_translation: We have to reduce the costs.
reduzieren.etymology_derivation: Soft Latin c shifted to German z [ts].

argumentieren.etymology_derivation: Directly derived from the Latin noun base argumentum + -ieren.

existieren.context_translation: The problem does not exist anymore.

fotografieren.context_translation: We are photographing the old houses.
fotografieren.etymology_derivation: A Greek-rooted international word in the -ieren loan-verb family; like all -ieren verbs its participle takes no ge-: fotografiert. [wiktionary]

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs NEVER take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert, reparieren → repariert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Adopted from Old French -ier in Middle High German as the universal productive suffix for foreign loan verbs.
